items.name: storyreel.life
items.brief: Three independent sources saw this and they disagree, which is the interesting part. Its pricing page went from two tiers to three while its US chart position slipped 45 to 47 and the number of countries it charts in halved from two to one. Adding a paid tier as attention narrows is a monetisation decision, not growth, and 31,066 ratings say the audience it has is already large enough to charge.
items.description: A short drama app, serving the vertical video serials that have grown into their own category: episodes of a minute or two, shot for a phone held upright, released in runs of fifty or more. The format is watched in a queue rather than sat down in front of, and the apps carrying it monetise by charging to unlock the next episode.

items.name: ottokit.com
items.brief: Downloads 3,152,066 to 3,176,891 in a day, which is 24,825 installations of a WordPress plugin in twenty four hours, against 90,000 sites running it. Traffic rank improved 2.0% over the same window, so two unrelated collectors moved together: one counting installs and one counting visits. The plugin also went from nine pricing tiers to ten, which is a company adjusting what it charges rather than what it ships.
items.description: A no code automation platform for WordPress, wiring the plugins a site already runs and the outside services it depends on into workflows without any glue code in between. It was called SureTriggers until the rename, and it sells against Zapier by living inside the site rather than calling it from outside.

still_moving.name: opslane.com
still_moving.brief: Stars 16 to 35 and HackerNews points 18 to 35 in a day, with comments 4 to 11, so comments grew faster than points, and open issues 7 to 9 behind them. Small numbers, and worth saying so: thirty five stars is a handful of people. What makes it worth a second look is that all four moved together on a project whose pitch is that it opens the pull request itself, which is a claim people either try or ignore.
still_moving.description: Error tracking that reads real user session recordings, works out which bugs are actually reaching users, and opens a pull request with a proposed fix rather than filing a ticket.

still_moving.name: magicpatterns.com
still_moving.brief: HackerNews points 51 to 55 and comments 23 to 25 while traffic rank improved 1.4% the same day. A modest move on all three, but the third one is the interesting one: attention on a link aggregator is cheap and people arriving at the site afterwards is not, and here the two moved together rather than one without the other.
still_moving.description: Generates production-ready interface code from a written prompt, working against your existing design system rather than a generic component library, so what comes out matches what you already ship.

still_moving.name: onepay.com
still_moving.brief: Go to market roles 4 to 5 on a board of 39, taking the sales and marketing share of hiring from 10.5% to 12.8%, while traffic rank improved 4.4% the same day. A company that has been hiring engineers beginning to hire sellers is the transition this whole method watches for. One role is thin evidence and the direction is what matters, but nobody posts a role they do not intend to pay for.
still_moving.description: OnePay is a US consumer mobile banking app offering saving, spending, borrowing, credit building and rewards in one account. It is backed by Walmart and aimed at customers underserved by traditional banks, competing with Cash App and Chime rather than with high-street lenders.

still_moving.name: SenteLabsAI/OpenExecutive
still_moving.brief: Stars 642 to 1,650 and forks 40 to 116 in a day, with HackerNews comments 283 to 656. Forks growing faster than stars means people are standing it up rather than bookmarking it, and open issues fell 12 to 5 across the same window. That is a maintainer keeping pace with the crowd rather than being buried by it.
still_moving.description: OpenExecutive is an AI-powered virtual executive team: a single coherent executive persona backed by eight specialist Claude agents, built on FastAPI with a Next.js front end. The idea is that a founder or small team can put a question to one "executive" and have it answered with the specialist reasoning of a full leadership bench behind it.
